learn.pageTitle: Doubling the Fu Equals One More Han in Mahjong Scoring
learn.pageDescription: One of the patterns hidden in the riichi mahjong scoring table: doubling the fu means the same for the score as adding one han, so 25 fu 2 han and 50 fu 1 han are both 1600 points.
learn.hanTitle: One more han doubles the score
learn.hanBody1: Scores come from a formula. For a non-dealer [[ron|ron]], it was the following.
learn.sourceNote: * This formula, and why the result is rounded up to the next 100 points, are covered in <link></link>
learn.hanBody2:
The han sits in the exponent of 2. Raising the exponent by one doubles the value, so each extra han doubles the score exactly.
Let us check this with a non-dealer ron at 30 fu.
learn.hanBody3:
The scores in the table go 1000 → 2000 → 3900 → 7700, which, if you look closely, drifts away from doubling.
That is because the result is rounded up to the next 100 points at the very end; the values before rounding keep doubling exactly all the way. The pattern is not broken.
learn.fuTitle: Doubling the fu does the same thing
learn.fuBody1:
Look at the formula once more. The [[fu|fu]] and the power of 2 are simply multiplied together.
Because it is a multiplication, doubling the fu and raising the power of 2 by one give the same product.
learn.fuBody2:
In other words, “the fu doubling” and “the han going up by one” mean exactly the same thing for the score. Rounding applies after the multiplication, so the scores in the table match exactly too.
First, let us look at the 25 fu of [[chiitoitsu|chiitoitsu]] and its double, 50 fu.
learn.linkedCellNote: * Colored cells have the same score. The 50 fu row is the 25 fu row shifted one han to the left
learn.fuBody3:
The sequence 1600 → 3200 → 6400 starts at 2 han for 25 fu and at 1 han for 50 fu. Only the starting position is shifted by one; the numbers themselves are the same.
The same happens with 30 fu and 60 fu, which you meet often with [[menzen|closed]] [[mentsute|standard hands]].
learn.fuBody4:
This is not limited to ron. Whether it is a [[tsumo|tsumo]] or a [[oya|dealer]] hand, every score comes from the same formula, so it shifts in the same way.
Let us check with the 20 fu of a [[pinfu|pinfu]] tsumo and its double, 40 fu.
learn.tsumoNote: * Tsumo scores: top = paid by each non-dealer / bottom = paid by the dealer
learn.fuBody5: However, only a few pairs of rows work this way. Fu go up in steps of 10 (25 fu is the only exception), so only the following five pairs have the doubled fu as an actual row in the table.
learn.manganTitle: Doubling works only up to just below mangan
learn.manganBody1:
This pattern holds only until the hand reaches [[mangan|mangan]]. Once the score reaches a certain size, it is capped at mangan, and beyond that point doubling the fu no longer changes the score.
The cells marked “Mangan” in the tables above are that boundary.
learn.manganBody2:
Still, the range below mangan is exactly where memorizing takes effort.
The scoring table has 11 fu rows, and five of them, 40, 50, 60, 80 and 100 fu, can be read off the row with half the fu by shifting one han. You do not need to memorize them anew.
learn.columnBody:
Some older rules count chiitoitsu as 50 fu 1 han instead of 25 fu 2 han.

That the two give the same score is no coincidence; it is exactly the pattern we just saw. 50 fu is double 25 fu, and 1 han is one less than 2 han, so they balance out.

Because fu and han can be traded like this, either way of counting lands on the same score.
